extracted.intended_audience: mathematics department chairs, MER organizers, mathematics educators, and policymakers involved in mathematics education reform
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation criteria and standards used to judge the effectiveness of the Mathematicians and Education Reform Forum (MER) at individual and departmental levels, focusing on workshops, networking, institutionalization, K-12 outreach, and systemic reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of workshops
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshop structure and execution (having an overarching theme, breakout sessions, informal contact time) that maximizes positive outcomes for participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshops are cited as MER's greatest strength; face-to-face exchanges, informal contact (e.g., meals), and a mix of plenary and breakout sessions help faculty 'gain insights about topics important to their departments' and generate spontaneous initiatives, collaborations, and idea 'bouncing'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental Network effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the Departmental Network facilitates departmental reform by bringing multiple faculty (including chairs) from a department to participate and by fostering inter-departmental interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departmental workshops appear to move more quickly toward systemic reform because key decision-makers (chairs) attend; having groups from each department increases likelihood of implementation and of pressuring central administration for resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual Network effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which MER's individual-oriented activities facilitate mathematicians’ participation in education reform at the personal level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by participants' reports that MER raised awareness, provided support/legitimization, and led to improved classroom pedagogy and changes in educational efforts; MER functions mainly as facilitator/supporter rather than originator of new ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of systemic reform (Jenness & Barley definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether MER encourages development of new working relationships within mathematics and among related disciplines, and whether broad changes have occurred within the mathematics community beyond local or individual change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systemic reform indicators include new inter-departmental collaborations, changes in attitudes across departments, involvement of administrative decision-makers, and emergence of programs that persist beyond individual champions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridges between mathematics and education departments
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent and nature of connections between math and education departments (joint appointments, co-PI roles, shared advising and committee service, redesigning teacher-course content to follow standards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include jointly appointed faculty, math educators serving as full math professors, faculty serving on education dissertations, and curriculum redesign aligned with NCTM standards. Such bridges indicate deeper institutional relationships supporting teacher preparation and reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutionalization / sustainability of initiatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether educational initiatives are supported by the department/university (not just by a few committed faculty), and whether programs would survive departures of individual champions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concern that pre-college/math outreach typically 'rests on the shoulders of very few faculty'; true institutional support (e.g., permanent appointments, center-directed initiatives) is necessary for systemic, sustainable reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional rewards for education involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition and reward structures (tenure and promotion, release time, respect, administrative support) for faculty engaged in educational reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: 'decent' teaching is necessary but not sufficient for tenure; few faculty have been promoted primarily for educational work; some departments have expanded consideration of educational endeavors in promotion decisions—such support is critical for sustained involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty awareness and engagement levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of faculty who have heard of MER and understand its implications; degree to which liaisons have spread awareness within departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report notes generally less than half had heard of MER and fewer than one-quarter understood the implications; awareness correlates with departmental interest in education and active liaison efforts; inviting 'cynics' to workshops can build credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of department chairs and leadership involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Involvement of chairs and departmental leaders in MER activities (attendance at workshops, follow-through), used as a strategic move to achieve broader acceptance within departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MER requested chair attendance at first meeting to increase acceptance; chairs help leverage resources from central administration; loss of a chair liaison (e.g., at Penn State) can weaken departmental ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: MER's function: facilitator/supporter vs initiator
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether MER primarily supports and legitimizes existing reform efforts rather than originating new initiatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants reported MER 'is a support mechanism for those members ... already involved in educational efforts' and helps take people where they are rather than forcing ideas; this conception of 'effective' guides the evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: K-12 outreach activity quality and types
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence and nature of outreach initiatives (in-service teacher enhancement, curriculum design projects, policy work), including longevity, follow-up, and networking among stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Regional Geometry Institute with year-round follow-up, TIMS curriculum project, centers that coordinate Statewide Systemic Initiatives. Quality includes teacher excitement, sustained contact, interdisciplinary networks, and clear links to departmental expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent and quality of inter-departmental collaborations
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurrence of collaborative projects across departments or institutions (planning grants, interdisciplinary initiatives) and the speed with which these collaborations form due to MER-facilitated contacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited outcomes include Nebraska-Oklahoma planning grant and multi-institution interdisciplinary initiatives emerging from workshops; MER helps speed interaction and planning that might otherwise be slower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation and uptake of actionable ideas (e.g., exchanges, internships)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether workshops produce concrete proposals (graduate/post-doctoral exchanges, internships, surveys, databases) and whether those proposals are taken up and implemented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: graduate/post-doctoral exchanges and departmental surveys to provide comparative information emerged from Santa Barbara and Austin workshops and showed promise of being implemented because chairs were present to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness and design of communication infrastructure (listserver/newsletter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design choices for MER's electronic and print communications (who is subscribed, moderation vs open access, traffic level) and their impact on diffusion and liaison burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original plan to subscribe only a few liaisons to moderate forwarding has merit but opening the list to any interested individual may relieve liaisons and not flood mailboxes, given low traffic observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimization of educational efforts within mathematics research community
rubrics_metrics.description: MER's ability to provide legitimacy by showing concrete examples of mathematicians engaged in reform, thereby making educational work more acceptable to peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimization is a noted strength; providing examples and a network gives faculty 'ammo' to advocate for changes and helps make pedagogy more acceptable at research universities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face-to-face versus internet-mediated interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative importance of in-person interactions compared with internet-based exchanges for effective networking and dissemination of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many participants valued face-to-face interactions as crucial to networking and idea development, though some suggested the Internet could realize many network benefits; workshops' informal social time was highlighted as important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurable reach and visibility of MER
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative indicators such as number of workshops, newsletter/mailing list size, advisory/task force composition, and participant demographics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documented metrics: approximately 18 workshops to date, over 750 people on the MER Newsletter mailing list, a 13-member Advisory Committee and 11-member Task Force; these provide indications of scale and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on teaching practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported changes in classroom pedagogy, adoption of standards (e.g., NCTM), and incorporation of cooperative learning or technology-based methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants reported improved classroom pedagogy and incorporation of ideas learned at MER workshops; example includes redesign of courses for elementary teachers to follow NCTM Standards and teaching with technology evaluated by education faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability of pre-college initiatives to personnel changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which K-12 initiatives depend on single individuals (risk if those individuals leave) versus being embedded institutionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penn State example: loss of a single faculty member led to collapse of outreach; only Texas-Austin showed strong institutional support via a mathematics educator on faculty—highlighting the need for structural supports to avoid fragility.
